text:
Looking at this footage: it's helmet-cam snowboarding video, not a talking-head podcast. The only substantive spoken content — the crew introductions, the plan to "meet at the bottom of this cliff," the alarmed "Oh, God!," and the caring "You okay?" check-in — all happens in the first 60 seconds. Past that point the transcript degenerates into the same line ("I'll try to follow you later") repeating for eight minutes straight, almost certainly a transcription artifact off ambient noise, and the frames I checked at 100s/250s/450s show visually interchangeable snowy descent with no standout action to justify pulling from later in the run.

That makes the first 60 seconds the genuine highlight: it's the only stretch with a real mini-arc (excited banter → dramatic reaction → reassurance) and it happens to end exactly on a sentence boundary — "...I'll try to follow you **later**." finishes at precisely 60.0s. I'll trim the timeline down to that span.

text:
The highlight is set: **0–60s** of the source, which is the only stretch of this 9-minute recording with real variation — everything from 60s onward on the transcript is the same line ("I'll try to follow you later") repeated for the remaining ~515 seconds, so there was nothing better to pull from later in the file. The kept 60 seconds carries a complete arc: the intro and radio-check ("Whoo! Tom... Ryan. Jennay. Say hi."), the plan ("Meeting at the bottom of this cliff"), the drop with a startled reaction ("Oh, God."), and the check-in afterward ("You okay?... I'll try to follow you later.").

Cut placement respects sentence boundaries — it starts at 0s (before any speech begins at 0.07s) and ends at exactly 60.00s, which lands right on the completed word "later." (59.38–60.00s); the next utterance doesn't begin until 60.07s, so nothing is severed mid-sentence.

This is a straightforward trim-to-highlight job with no captions, transitions, or grading requested, so no further edits are needed. The result has been visually confirmed via get_frame at 40s; I have not screened every second of the 60s window, so if you want a final pass I'd suggest a quick playback check on the "Oh, God." and "You okay?" moments specifically, but the cut structure itself is complete and sentence-safe.
